source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: In a reversible chemical process sitting at dynamic equilibrium, the forward rate compared with the reverse rate is
options: much larger for the forward step
much larger for the reverse step
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium means both reactions continue, but their rates match so there is no net change.

questions.stem: Once chemical equilibrium is established in a closed vessel, the amounts of reactants and products
options: become constant, though not necessarily equal
keep rising until the vessel is full
fall to zero for the reactants
questions.explanation: Equilibrium concentrations stay constant with time. Equality of concentrations is not required.

questions.stem: A true chemical equilibrium can be approached
options: from either the reactant side or the product side
only by starting with pure reactants
only by starting with pure products
only after a catalyst is added
questions.explanation: The same equilibrium state is reached whether one begins with reactants or with products, at a given temperature.

questions.stem: A necessary condition for a chemical equilibrium to be set up is that the reacting system remains
options: at a pressure of 1 atm only
questions.explanation: Matter must not leave or enter; otherwise concentrations never settle to a true equilibrium.

questions.stem: At chemical equilibrium the colour, density and other bulk properties of the mixture
options: become identical to those of the pure reactant
questions.explanation: Macroscopic properties are constant at equilibrium even though molecules still react microscopically.

questions.stem: The dynamic character of chemical equilibrium is shown by the observation that
options: forward and reverse reactions continue at equal speeds
questions.explanation: Isotopic tracing shows both directions remain active; their rates are equal, so composition is steady.

questions.stem: Introducing a catalyst into a gaseous mixture that is already at equilibrium
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds both directions equally. K and the equilibrium amounts stay the same; only the time to reach equilibrium falls.

questions.stem: The numerical size of an equilibrium constant informs us about
options: how far the reaction proceeds, not how rapidly it occurs
the molecularity of the slow step
questions.explanation: K measures the extent of reaction at equilibrium. Rate is a kinetic quantity and is not given by K.

questions.stem: For a reaction at chemical equilibrium at constant temperature and pressure, the change in Gibbs energy $\Delta G$ is
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is the state of minimum G at given T and P, so $\Delta G = 0$. $\Delta G^\circ$ is related to K and need not be zero.

questions.stem: A sealed flask holds N2, H2 and NH3 already at equilibrium. Ammonia molecules in that flask
options: keep forming and decomposing at equal rates
are converted entirely back into N2 and H2
increase steadily because the vessel is closed
questions.explanation: Closure keeps the total amounts fixed, but the Haber reactions remain active in both directions at matching rates.

questions.stem: According to the law of mass action, $K_c$ for $a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}$ is
questions.explanation: Kc is the quotient of product active masses over reactant active masses, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

questions.stem: The standard relation connecting $K_p$ and $K_c$ for a gas reaction is
questions.explanation: Partial pressures and concentrations are linked by $p = CRT$, which produces the factor $(RT)^{\Delta n}$.

questions.stem: In $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, the exponent $\Delta n$ is
options: gaseous moles of products minus gaseous moles of reactants
total moles of all species including solids
the molecularity of the forward step
questions.explanation: Only gaseous species contribute to $\Delta n$ because Kp is built from partial pressures.

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{H_2}(g) + \mathrm{I_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(g)$, $K_p$ compared with $K_c$ is
questions.explanation: There are two moles of gas on each side, so $\Delta n = 0$ and $K_p = K_c$.

questions.stem: For the Haber equation $\mathrm{N_2}(g) + 3\mathrm{H_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}(g)$, $\Delta n$ in the $K_p$–$K_c$ formula is
questions.explanation: Gaseous moles: products 2, reactants 4, so $\Delta n = 2 - 4 = -2$.

questions.stem: A very large numerical value of $K_c$ for a reaction means that at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Large K means the numerator (products) is much greater than the denominator (reactants) at equilibrium.

questions.stem: If the equilibrium constant of a written reaction is $K$, the equilibrium constant of the reverse writing is
questions.explanation: Reversing the reaction inverts the concentration quotient, so the constant becomes $1/K$.

questions.stem: If a balanced chemical equation is multiplied through by 2, the new equilibrium constant is
questions.explanation: Each concentration is raised to twice the original power, which squares the original K.

questions.stem: Active mass in the law of mass action, for a dilute solution, is taken as the
questions.explanation: For solutions the active mass is the molarity (mol L^{-1}), often written in square brackets.

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{PCl_5}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3}(g) + \mathrm{Cl_2}(g)$, the value of $\Delta n$ is
questions.explanation: Two moles of gas appear from one mole, so $\Delta n = +1$.

questions.stem: The SI-style units of $K_c$ for $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}$ are
questions.explanation: Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2][H2]^3) has concentration units of (mol L^{-1})^{-2}, i.e. L^2 mol^{-2}.

questions.stem: The $K_c$ expression for $2\mathrm{SO_2}(g) + \mathrm{O_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}(g)$ is
questions.explanation: Products over reactants with stoichiometric exponents: two for SO3, two for SO2, one for O2.

questions.stem: Whenever $\Delta n = 0$ for a gas-phase equilibrium, $K_p$ and $K_c$ are
questions.explanation: $(RT)^{\Delta n} = 1$ when $\Delta n = 0$, so the two constants coincide numerically.

questions.stem: The constant $K_p$ built from partial pressures is the natural choice for
questions.explanation: Kp uses partial pressures, so it applies to equilibria in which gases appear.

questions.stem: At $300\ \mathrm{K}$, for a gas reaction with $\Delta n = +1$ and $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}$, the ratio $K_p/K_c$ equals about
For $\mathrm{A}(g) + \mathrm{B}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}(g)$, equilibrium concentrations are $[\mathrm{A}] = 1$, $[\mathrm{B}] = 1$, $[\mathrm{C}] = 2$ (all in mol L^{-1}). $K_c$ is

For $\mathrm{PCl_5} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3} + \mathrm{Cl_2}$, $K_c = 0.04\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$. If $[\mathrm{PCl_3}] = [\mathrm{Cl_2}] = 0.20\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$, the equilibrium $[\mathrm{PCl_5}]$ is
The equilibrium $2\mathrm{HI} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{I_2}$ has $K_c = 0.25$. Starting with $1.0$ mol HI in a $1.0$ L bulb, the equilibrium amount of H2 is
If $K_1$ is the constant for $\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{B}$ and $K_2$ for $\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}$, the constant for $\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.explanation: The overall quotient is the product of the stepwise quotients, so overall $K = K_1 K_2$.

questions.stem: For Haber synthesis $\Delta n = -2$, so at a given temperature $K_p$ is
questions.explanation: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2} = K_c/(RT)^2$, hence $K_p < K_c$ at ordinary T where $RT > 1$ in L atm mol^{-1}.

questions.stem: At $500\ \mathrm{K}$ with $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}$, a gas reaction has $\Delta n = -1$. The ratio $K_c/K_p$ equals
The reaction $2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}$ has $K_c = 4$. For $\mathrm{SO_3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SO_2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}$, the new $K_c$ is
questions.explanation: Reversing gives $1/4$. Halving the equation takes the square root: $\sqrt{1/4} = 1/2$.

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{PCl_5}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3}(g) + \mathrm{Cl_2}(g)$ at $300\ \mathrm{K}$, $K_p = 24.6\ \mathrm{atm}$. With $R = 0.082\ \mathrm{L\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}$, $K_c$ in mol L^{-1} is
Given $2\mathrm{NO}(g) + \mathrm{O_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}(g)$ with $K_c = 100$, the constant for $\mathrm{NO_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NO}(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g)$ is
questions.explanation: The target equation is the reverse of the original, halved. New $K = 1/\sqrt{100} = 0.10$.

questions.stem: An equilibrium in which every participating species is in the same physical state is called
questions.explanation: Homogeneous equilibrium: one phase throughout, e.g. all gases or all aqueous species.

questions.stem: Thermal decomposition of limestone $\mathrm{CaCO_3}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(s) + \mathrm{CO_2}(g)$ is classified as
questions.explanation: Solids and a gas coexist, so more than one phase is present: heterogeneous.

questions.stem: When $K_c$ is written for a heterogeneous equilibrium, concentrations of pure solids are
options: replaced by their densities in g mL^{-1}
set equal to the total pressure
questions.explanation: The active mass of a pure solid is constant and is absorbed into K, so solids do not appear in the K expression.

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{CaCO_3}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(s) + \mathrm{CO_2}(g)$, $K_p$ reduces to
questions.explanation: Both solids drop out, leaving $K_p = p_{CO_2}$. At a fixed temperature the CO2 pressure is fixed.

questions.stem: Pure liquid water is left out of many $K_c$ expressions because its concentration is
questions.explanation: The molarity of the pure liquid is fixed (~55.5 mol L^{-1}) and is built into the constant.

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}(s) + 4\mathrm{H_2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\mathrm{Fe}(s) + 4\mathrm{H_2O}(g)$, $K_c$ is
questions.explanation: Pure solids Fe3O4 and Fe are omitted. Only the four moles of steam and hydrogen remain.

questions.stem: Dumping extra solid CaO into a vessel where $\mathrm{CaCO_3}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(s) + \mathrm{CO_2}(g)$ is already at equilibrium
options: does not change the equilibrium CO2 pressure
raises $p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$ in proportion to the mass added
forces all CO2 back to carbonate
questions.explanation: K_p = p_CO2 depends only on temperature. Extra pure solid does not alter that pressure.

questions.stem: At a fixed temperature, increasing the amount of CaCO3(s) in a closed crucible containing CaO(s) and CO2(g) at equilibrium does not raise $p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$ because
options: $K_p = p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}$ is a function of T alone
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous K_p contains only p_CO2. Once both solids are present, that pressure is fixed by T.

questions.stem: The degree of dissociation $\alpha$ of a substance is the
options: fraction of the original molecules that have dissociated
number of moles of product only
questions.explanation: $\alpha$ = (moles that dissociate) / (moles taken initially). It is a fraction, often between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: Starting with 1 mol of PCl5 that dissociates as $\mathrm{PCl_5} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3} + \mathrm{Cl_2}$, the total number of moles at equilibrium is
questions.explanation: PCl5 left = $1-\alpha$; PCl3 = $\alpha$; Cl2 = $\alpha$; sum = $1+\alpha$.

questions.stem: The numerical value of the degree of dissociation $\alpha$ always lies between
questions.explanation: None dissociated: $\alpha = 0$. Completely dissociated: $\alpha = 1$.

questions.stem: For the gas reaction $\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{B} + \mathrm{C}$ starting with 1 mol of A in volume $V$, $K_c$ equals
questions.explanation: [B] = [C] = $\alpha/V$, [A] = $(1-\alpha)/V$, so $K_c = (\alpha/V)^2 / ((1-\alpha)/V) = \alpha^2/((1-\alpha)V)$.

questions.stem: If the theoretical vapour density of undissociated N2O4 is $D$ and the observed vapour density is $d$, then $\alpha$ for $\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}$ is
questions.explanation: For $n = 2$, $\alpha = (D - d)/((n-1)d) = (D - d)/d$. Observed density falls as more moles form.

questions.stem: Ostwald's dilution law connects the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte with
options: its concentration and the ionisation constant
the boiling point of the solvent
questions.explanation: For a weak binary electrolyte, $K_a \approx \alpha^2 C$, so $\alpha$ rises as the solution is diluted.

questions.stem: One mole of N2O4 that is $\alpha$-dissociated according to $\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}$ produces a total of
questions.explanation: N2O4 left = $1-\alpha$; NO2 = $2\alpha$; total = $1+\alpha$.

questions.stem: If PCl5 is fifty percent dissociated at equilibrium, the value of $\alpha$ to substitute in $K_c$ formulae is
questions.explanation: Fifty percent means half the original molecules have split, so $\alpha = 0.50$ (not 50).

questions.stem: For $\mathrm{PCl_5} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3} + \mathrm{Cl_2}$, $K_p$ in terms of $\alpha$ and the total pressure $P$ is
questions.explanation: Mole fractions give $p_{PCl3} = p_{Cl2} = \alpha P/(1+\alpha)$ and $p_{PCl5} = (1-\alpha)P/(1+\alpha)$, whence $K_p = \alpha^2 P/(1-\alpha^2)$.

questions.stem: Raising the total pressure on $\mathrm{N_2O_4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}(g)$ causes the degree of dissociation to
questions.explanation: The product side has more moles of gas, so Le Chatelier predicts less dissociation at higher P.

questions.stem: A 1 L flask is charged with 1 mol of A, which dissociates as $\mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{B}$ with $\alpha = 0.50$. $K_c$ is
For $\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}$ at total pressure $1\ \mathrm{atm}$, $K_p = 4/3\ \mathrm{atm}$. The degree of dissociation $\alpha$ is
questions.explanation: $K_p = 4\alpha^2 P/(1-\alpha^2)$. With $P = 1$ and $K_p = 4/3$, $4\alpha^2 = (4/3)(1-\alpha^2)$ gives $\alpha = 1/2$.

questions.stem: In the Haber equilibrium $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, raising the total pressure at constant T shifts the mixture
questions.explanation: Fewer moles of gas sit on the ammonia side, so high pressure favours NH3.

questions.stem: Haber synthesis of ammonia is exothermic. Raising the temperature at equilibrium therefore
questions.explanation: Heat is a product of the forward Haber step. Extra heat drives the endothermic reverse reaction.

questions.stem: The iron catalyst used in Haber synthesis
options: does not change the equilibrium yield of NH3
questions.explanation: The catalyst shortens the time to equilibrium without altering K or the equilibrium composition.

questions.stem: Admission of an inert gas at constant volume to a gaseous equilibrium mixture
options: does not shift the equilibrium position
questions.explanation: Partial pressures of the reacting gases stay the same at constant V and T, so the position is unchanged.

questions.stem: Admission of an inert gas at constant pressure to $\mathrm{PCl_5} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl_3} + \mathrm{Cl_2}$
options: shifts the equilibrium toward greater dissociation
questions.explanation: The volume must increase to keep P fixed, which dilutes the gases and favours the side with more moles.

questions.stem: Adding extra nitrogen to a Haber mixture at constant volume
questions.explanation: Increasing a reactant concentration drives the net reaction toward products until Q again equals K.

questions.stem: The Contact oxidation $2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}$ is favoured by
options: high pressure and a moderately low temperature
low pressure and very high temperature
low pressure and a catalyst only
questions.explanation: $\Delta n$ is negative and the forward reaction is exothermic, so high P and moderate T help SO3.

questions.stem: Liquefying and removing ammonia as it forms in the Haber converter
options: drives the net reaction toward more NH3
is forbidden by Le Chatelier's principle
questions.explanation: Removing a product lowers Q, so the system makes more product to restore equilibrium.

questions.stem: For an endothermic dissociation already at equilibrium, heating the mixture
questions.explanation: Heat is a reactant of an endothermic step, so extra heat is consumed by forming more products.

questions.stem: Compressing the volume of an $\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}$ mixture at constant T
questions.explanation: The left side has fewer moles of gas, so a smaller volume (higher P) favours N2O4.

questions.stem: Typical industrial Haber conditions taught at Intermediate level are about
questions.explanation: High pressure favours NH3; a compromise temperature near 450 °C with an Fe catalyst gives a usable rate.

questions.stem: The solid catalyst employed in the Contact process for sulphur trioxide is
questions.explanation: Vanadium(V) oxide is the Contact-process catalyst; it does not change the equilibrium constant.

questions.stem: A very high temperature is avoided in Haber manufacture even though the rate would rise, because
options: the equilibrium yield of ammonia falls
questions.explanation: The forward Haber reaction is exothermic, so K falls as T rises and less NH3 is present at equilibrium.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature of the Contact equilibrium $2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO_3}$ (exothermic forward)
options: shifts the mixture toward SO2 and O2
questions.explanation: Heat is a product of SO3 formation, so extra heat is absorbed by the reverse reaction.

questions.stem: Enriching a Contact-process mixture with extra oxygen at constant T and V
options: increases the equilibrium amount of SO3
has no effect because O2 is a catalyst
forces all SO3 back to SO2
questions.explanation: Adding a reactant drives the net reaction forward until Q = K once more.

questions.stem: For the dissociation of PCl5, the degree of dissociation $\alpha$ falls when the pressure is raised because
options: the product side has more moles of gas
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier: extra pressure is relieved by forming fewer gas molecules, i.e. undissociated PCl5.

questions.stem: A compromise temperature is chosen for Haber synthesis because
options: low T favours yield but makes the reaction slow
high T always maximises both yield and rate
questions.explanation: K is larger at low T (exothermic) but molecules react slowly; ~450 °C with a catalyst is the industrial compromise.

questions.stem: Adding argon at constant pressure to Haber gas, as opposed to adding it at constant volume,
options: shifts the equilibrium toward N2 and H2
has the same (null) effect as constant-volume addition
questions.explanation: Constant-P dilution increases volume and favours the side with more moles (reactants). Constant-V addition of inert gas does not shift the position.

questions.stem: If both the pressure is increased and the temperature is lowered on a Haber mixture already at equilibrium, the ammonia yield
options: rises, because both changes favour NH3
falls, because the two changes cancel
is unaffected because K is constant
questions.explanation: High P favours the fewer-moles side (NH3) and low T favours the exothermic forward step. Both act in the same direction.

questions.stem: Compare inert-gas addition to Haber gas: constant volume versus constant pressure. The equilibrium shifts backward only in the
questions.explanation: At constant V partial pressures of N2, H2 and NH3 are unchanged. At constant P the mixture expands, favouring more moles (N2 + H2).

questions.stem: Arrhenius defined an acid as a substance that, in water, furnishes
questions.explanation: In the Arrhenius picture an acid ionises in water to give H+ (more precisely H3O+).

questions.stem: According to Arrhenius, a base dissolved in water produces
questions.explanation: Arrhenius bases (NaOH, KOH) release hydroxide ions in aqueous solution.

questions.stem: In the Bronsted–Lowry sense an acid is a
questions.explanation: Bronsted acids donate H+. This definition also covers non-aqueous proton transfers.

questions.stem: In the Bronsted–Lowry sense a base is a
questions.explanation: A Bronsted base accepts H+. Ammonia is a base even though it has no hydroxide to start with.

questions.stem: A Lewis acid is defined as an
questions.explanation: Lewis acids (BF3, AlCl3, H+) have a vacant orbital and accept a lone pair.

questions.stem: A Lewis base is defined as an
questions.explanation: Lewis bases (NH3, H2O, Cl-) have a lone pair available for sharing.

questions.stem: BF3 is classified as a Lewis acid because the boron atom
options: is electron-deficient and can accept a lone pair
donates a lone pair to fluorine
questions.explanation: Boron in BF3 has only six electrons in its valence shell and accepts a pair from a base.

questions.stem: Ammonia acts as a Lewis base because the nitrogen atom
options: carries a lone pair that can be donated
questions.explanation: The lone pair on N is donated to H+ or to a Lewis acid such as BF3.

questions.stem: A limitation of Arrhenius theory is that it
questions.explanation: Arrhenius acids and bases are defined through H+ and OH- in water, so the theory is silent on gas-phase or non-aqueous proton transfer.

questions.stem: The gas-phase combination of HCl with NH3 to give solid NH4Cl is accounted for by
options: Bronsted proton transfer, not by the Arrhenius definition
questions.explanation: No water is present, so Arrhenius language does not apply. HCl donates a proton to NH3 (Bronsted).

questions.stem: AlCl3 behaves as a Lewis acid in many organic reactions because aluminium
options: is electron-deficient and accepts a lone pair
questions.explanation: Al in AlCl3 has a vacant orbital. It accepts a pair from a chloride ion or from a π bond.

questions.stem: Which of the following species is amphiprotic?
questions.explanation: HCO3- can donate a proton (to give CO3^{2-}) or accept one (to give H2CO3).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a Lewis acid?
questions.explanation: NH3 donates a lone pair, so it is a Lewis base. BF3, AlCl3 and H+ accept pairs.

questions.stem: In the adduct-forming step $\mathrm{BF_3} + \mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_3N{\text{–}}BF_3}$, the bond created is a
options: coordinate bond, with BF3 as Lewis acid and NH3 as Lewis base
ionic bond between F- and NH4+
questions.explanation: Nitrogen donates its lone pair into the vacant orbital on boron: a coordinate (dative) Lewis acid–base bond.

questions.stem: Taking hydrochloric acid of concentration $0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$ as fully ionised, its pH is
questions.explanation: For a strong monobasic acid, $[H+] = 0.01 = 10^{-2}$, so $\mathrm{pH} = 2$.

questions.stem: A nitric acid sample whose molarity is $10^{-3}$ has a hydrogen-ion exponent of
questions.explanation: HNO3 is strong, so $[H+] = 10^{-3}$ and pH = 3.

questions.stem: Complete ionisation of a $0.1$ molar HCl sample produces a pH equal to
Sodium hydroxide at $0.01\ \mathrm{M}$ is a strong base; the pOH of this liquor is
The pH corresponding to a $0.01$ molar NaOH solution at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is
questions.explanation: pOH = 2 and pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 12.

questions.stem: Potassium hydroxide of molarity $10^{-3}$ at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ registers a pH of
questions.explanation: pOH = 3, therefore pH = 14 − 3 = 11.

questions.stem: The ionic product of water $K_w$ at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is
At $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the sum of pH and pOH of any aqueous solution is
questions.explanation: pH + pOH = pKw = 14 when Kw = 10^{-14}.

questions.stem: Pure water at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is neutral because $[H+] = [OH-]$; its pH is therefore
questions.explanation: $[H+] = 10^{-7}$ in pure water at 25 °C, so pH = 7. Neutrality means [H+] = [OH-], not a fixed number at every T.

questions.stem: A strong acid such as HCl in dilute aqueous solution is regarded as
questions.explanation: Strong acids are fully dissociated, so [H+] equals the analytical concentration (unless extremely dilute).

questions.stem: If the pH of a solution is 4, the hydrogen-ion concentration is
questions.explanation: By definition $[H+] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: Among the following, the strong bases commonly used in Intermediate calculations are
questions.explanation: Alkali-metal hydroxides are fully ionised. Aqueous ammonia is a weak base.

questions.stem: Treating dilute sulphuric acid as fully providing two H+ per formula unit, a $0.005\ \mathrm{M}$ H2SO4 bath has pH about
questions.explanation: $[H+] \approx 2 \times 0.005 = 0.010$, so pH = 2.

questions.stem: A $0.05\ \mathrm{M}$ NaOH solution at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ has pOH = 1.3; its pH is therefore about
Equal volumes of $0.20\ \mathrm{M}$ HCl and $0.20\ \mathrm{M}$ NaOH are mixed. The pH of the resulting liquor is
questions.explanation: Equimolar strong acid and strong base cancel. The mixture is a solution of NaCl, which is neutral at 25 °C.

questions.stem: Barium hydroxide of concentration $0.005\ \mathrm{M}$ supplies two OH- per formula unit. Its pOH is
If a solution has pH = 3, the hydroxide-ion concentration at $25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is
Kw of water increases as the temperature is raised. The pH of pure water at 50 °C is therefore
options: less than 7, yet the water remains neutral
greater than 7 and the water is alkaline
questions.explanation: Both [H+] and [OH-] rise equally when Kw rises, so the liquid is still neutral, but pH = −log[H+] falls below 7.

questions.stem: Fifty millilitres of $0.10\ \mathrm{M}$ hydrochloric acid is combined with fifty millilitres of $0.10\ \mathrm{M}$ nitric acid. The pH of the blend is
questions.explanation: Each acid contributes 5 mmol of H+. Total H+ = 10 mmol in 100 mL, so [H+] = 0.10 and pH = 1.0.

questions.stem: Thirty millilitres of $0.10\ \mathrm{M}$ HCl is mixed with twenty millilitres of $0.10\ \mathrm{M}$ NaOH. The pH of the leftover acidic solution is about
questions.explanation: H+ supplied = 3.0 mmol; OH- = 2.0 mmol. Excess H+ = 1.0 mmol in 50 mL, so [H+] = 0.020 and pH = 1.7.

questions.stem: A weak acid in water is only
questions.explanation: Weak acids establish an equilibrium HA ⇌ H+ + A-; a large fraction of HA remains undissociated.

questions.stem: The acid dissociation constant $K_a$ of a weak acid HA is
questions.explanation: Ka is the equilibrium constant of HA ⇌ H+ + A-, with water omitted as the solvent.

questions.stem: Among acids of the same type, the larger the $K_a$
options: the larger the pKa always means stronger
questions.explanation: A bigger Ka means a larger fraction is ionised at equilibrium, so the acid is stronger.

questions.stem: Ostwald's approximation for a weak acid of concentration C is $\alpha \approx$
questions.explanation: From $K_a = \alpha^2 C/(1-\alpha) \approx \alpha^2 C$ when $\alpha \ll 1$, so $\alpha \approx \sqrt{K_a/C}$.

questions.stem: The familiar Intermediate example of a weak monobasic acid is
questions.explanation: CH3COOH is only slightly ionised in water (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10^{-5}). HCl, HNO3 and HClO4 are strong.

questions.stem: Aqueous ammonia (NH4OH) is treated in Intermediate chemistry as a
questions.explanation: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH- has a small Kb, so ammonia is a weak base.

questions.stem: The base ionisation constant $K_b$ of a weak base B is written
questions.explanation: For B + H2O ⇌ BH+ + OH-, $K_b = [BH+][OH-]/[B]$.

questions.stem: The quantity pKa of a weak acid is defined as
questions.explanation: pKa = −log Ka, analogous to pH = −log[H+].

questions.stem: A smaller pKa corresponds to
options: a stronger conjugate base always being more concentrated
a larger pH of the pure acid always
questions.explanation: Small pKa means large Ka, hence a stronger acid.
